newsitem.title: UK: Ashanti sees stable earnings per share.
newsitem.headline: Ashanti sees stable earnings per share.

text.p: Ashanti Goldfields, the Ghanaian gold mine, said on Tuesday that it expected earnings per share to be stable in the 1997 financial year.
"It will be about the same," finance director Mark Keatly told journalists.
In the 12 months to September 30, 1996, earnings per share fell to $0.79 from $1.22 due to rising costs and the issue of new shares for acquisitions.
No new share issues are planned for 1997, though operating costs will continue to rise to about $270 per ounce of gold compared with $248 in the year to September 30, Keatly said.
Ashanti, privatised in 1994 and the flagship of Ghana's economy, will change its reporting period, making it coincide with a calendar year from January 1.
In the 12 months to September 30, total costs were driven higher by rising labour and cyanide prices, used for leaching, which saw increases by more than 60 percent over the last 15 months.

Ashanti, in which Britain's Lonrho has a 33.6 percent stake, in May agreed to a 100 percent pay rise in local currency terms with its Ghanainan workers after their wage increases had previously lagged those at other mines.
The wage rise was 40 percent in dollar terms, which was more than Ashanti had expected due to a relatively strong local currency, Keatly said.
"That hurt us in the short term," he said.
Costs will be pushed further upwards in 1997 because of lower grade surface mining at Ashanti's biggest operation: the Obuasi mine.
This will offset measures to reduce labour costs, such as reducing overtime compensation and cutting the total number of workers to less than 12,000 from a current 13,500.
But costs are seen pushed back to $250 per ounce in 1998, when the cost cutting measures start to bite and more of Obuasi's production comes from high grade underground reserves.
Obuasi's overall production is seen declining to 800,000 ounces from 883,853 as Ashanti abandons its goal of one million ounce production.
"We are changing our focus from an emphasis on the one million ounce target by focusing on both production and costs," said Trevor Schulz, chief operating officer.

Production for the group as a whole is set to increase to 1.1 million ounces in 1997, 1.2 million in 1998 and 1.4 million in the year thereafter. Production in the year to September 30 was 0.9 million ounces.
Ashanti hedged 85 percent of its 1997 gold production at $420 per ounce after a similar policy helped cushion the profit fall in the last 12-month period.
"The hedging programme will continue to give us good cash margins," said Keatly.
The hedging policy is aimed at protecting Ashanti's investments plans, he added.

Capital expenditure is scheduled to rise to $255 million in 1997 from 196.6 million in the year to September 30. About half of the 255 million is earmarked for developments of the Bibiani project in Ghana and the Siguiri project in Guinea.
Capital expenditure at Obuasi will decline from $145 million in the year to September 30 to $110 million in calendar 1997 to 100 million in 1998.
"We really have broken the back of capex at Obuasi," said Keatly.
Ashanti earlier reported that earnings after tax and minorities fell to $70.9 million from $105.9 million, coming in below analysts' expectations.
-- Hans de Jongh, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
